nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
COMMON NAME:  Silver Perch
SPECIES:  Bairdiella chrysoura

nodes.title: CLASSIFICATION
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
	Class: Osteichthyes
	Order: 	Perciformes
	Family: Sciaenidae

Other Common Names:  butterfish (664); yellowtail (255 312 378 581 664 834); perch, white perch, sand perch, yellow finned perch (312 834); silver croaker (791); sugar trout (1056); Virginia perch, mademoiselle, tint (312).

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Generally too small in size to support a commercial fishery (834).  No special fishery exists because stocks have declined in recent years (791), and Florida landings data do not list the species separately (902).  Caught with pound nets, seines and bottom trawls, but only occasionally marketed for human consumption (791).  Hildebrand and Schroeder (312) reported that in the early 1920's, small quantities of larger fish were sold in the markets at Norfolk and Baltimore.

Recreational:  Caught by sport fishermen by hook and line, but used mostly for bait (791). Considered an excellent pan fish comparable to Spot (834).

Ecological Role:  In several systems the silver perch may become a dominant species (648) and therefore have an enormous effect on the ecology of a system.

Indicator:  Hansen and Wilson (272) recorded concentrations of DDT and its metabolites from .02 to 1.26 in 0 class fish from Pensacola estuary.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  In the western Atlantic from Massachusetts and Connecticut to southern Florida, and in the eastern and northern Gulf of Mexico from Florida to northern Mexico (788 791).  Very abundant from New Jersey to central Florida .  In the northern Gulf of Mexico,  Hoese and Moore (327) reported that silver perch are more common to saltier bays, with young occurring in grass beds, which might indicate a greater abundance toward south Texas.

Within Study Area:  Common in nearshore and estuarine waters throughout Florida, with young found mostly in estuarine grass beds (993), also reported from fresh waters (791 1037).  Abundant year round in Charlotte Harbor (789), and common especially during warmer months in Tampa Bay and at Cedar Key (581 664).  Found throughout the Indian River Lagoon, but the largest abundance occurs in the north and central part of the lagoon (993 997 1195 1196 1242) with very few occurring in the southern end of the Indian River Lagoon (887).

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body: Eggs are pelagic (392 415), larvae pelagic to demersal, juveniles and adults are demersal (363).

nodes.title: Movement/Migration
nodes.body: Silver Perch adults move to deeper bay waters and offshore in winter, returning to the estuarine feeding and nursery grounds in the spring and summer to spawn (171 255 791).  In the Maryland _ Virginia area, most commonly taken in the bays from May through October (312 886 1057).  Abundant in North Carolina sounds and estuaries from early spring to late fall (834).  Juveniles move into the shallow back bays (255).  In Tampa Bay, young appear in Boca Ciega Bay in May; by June, they begin to appear in Tampa Bay while remaining fairly abundant in Boca Ciega Bay.  Numbers taken in Tampa Bay increase considerably in July, and begin decreasing by August; most are gone from the bay by November (664).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type:  Eggs may be estuarine to marine depending on where they are spawned (363).  Adults most common in bays and quiet lagoons, especially estuaries (171).  Reid (581) considered the species to be primarily an open water inhabitant at Cedar Key.

Substrate:  Adults over mud and sand bottoms (602 791).  Juveniles found along shore zone rivers in ditches, in lower portions of marsh creeks over mud and sand bottoms (725) often over heavy detritus (313); young usually occur in grass bed areas (327).

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body: Larvae have been taken in temperatures from 16.4 - 31.8 (354).  In Charlotte Harbor, small specimens (11 - 25 mm SL) were taken at 16.1 C (789).   Juveniles have been taken in temperatures ranging from 4.8 C (725) to 32.5 C (664).  Adults have been collected at temperatures from 10.0 - 34.5 C (255 603 789).  Springer and Woodburn (664) reported cold killed individuals in Tampa Bay when water temperature was recorded as 13.0 C, however Gilmore et al. (236) reported none killed in an Indian River Lagoon hypothermal mortality where minimum temperatures ranged from 6 to 13 C.

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body: Larvae have been taken at salinities from 2.0 (1007) to 37.4 ppt (363).  Juveniles and/or adults found in several locations at salinities from 0.0 (264 725 789 848 885 1043) to 35.0 ppt (255 581 664 751 789).  Adults are euryhaline, taken in salinities from 0.0 - 48.0 ppt (171 255 751 1043).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body: Reproductive Mode:  The species is dioecious with broadcast spawning and external fertilization.

nodes.title: Mating/Spawning
nodes.body:
As with most of the drums sound produced by special muscles inserted at the swim bladder wall are believed to play a role in the spawning activity (246 1058 1059).  Spawning probably occurs in primary bays and passes (255 313 614 664 725 1058), but may also occur offshore to some extent since eggs have been collected there (116 313).  Reported season is March through May in Tampa Bay (664), May to September in northern Florida (581), April through June in Louisiana (252 614 751), and the spring in Texas (255).  Gilmore (1271) has heard male spawning sounds during all months of the year.  Spawning peaks may occur in spring and late summer (116).  In the Atlantic, spawning occurs in New Jersey from June through August with a peak in June (762), in the spring and early summer (May - July) in Delaware and Chesapeake Bays (312 368), and in April through mid-July in North Carolina (313).  It has been suggested that spawning occurs in the early evening before 8 o'clock (393).  Ripe individuals or eggs collected at 14.3 - 26.0 ppt and 19.40 C - 28.0 C (363).

Fecundity: A 140 mm female was reported to contain 52,000 eggs (312).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg/Larvae:  Range of total egg diameter 0.66 - 0.88mm (mean 0.69 - 0.83mm) (368).  Eggs reported to hatch in about 18 hours at 27.0 C (393), and in 40 - 50 hours at 19.0 to 21.0 C (762).  Yolksac larvae hatch at 1.5 - 1.9 mm (762).  Two days after hatching yolk sac completely absorbed, and larvae measure 2.5 - 2.8 mm (392 762).  Notochord flexion begins at 3.5 - 5.0 mm and is completed by 7.0 - 8.0 mm (392).

Juveniles/Adults:  The juvenile stage is attained around 10 mm TL (392).  Juveniles exhibit growth rates of about 15 mm/month from May to November (116).  Hildebrand and Cable (313) reported the following average lengths at Beaufort:  June, 8.7 mm; July, 31.9 mm; September, 81 mm; February 117.5 mm.  The following lengths were reported from Beaufort and the Chesapeake areas: first winter, 60 - 140 mm; second winter, 120 - 200 mm; and third season at spawning, 150 - 210 mm (392).  Some individuals may mature at the end of their first year (313) but most mature during their second year (762).  Reported size at maturity 130 - 140 mm (255 313) to 150 - 210 mm (470 762).  Frequently reach a size of 240 mm (327 762), and largest individual reported as 300 mm (788).  May live up to 6 years (762).  Another study, conducted in Mexico, reports the maximum age as 13 months (Chavance et al. 1984)

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Silver Perch larvae and small juveniles consume mostly copepods (163).  Larger juveniles and adults are primarily carnivores, feeding mainly on small crustaceans and benthic invertebrates, and occasionally on small fishes (163 179 241 312 581 664 791).

	Order: 	Perciformes
	Family: Sciaenidae

Other Common Names:  butterfish (664); yellowtail (255 312 378 581 664 834); perch, white perch, sand perch, yellow finned perch (312 834); silver croaker (791); sugar trout (1056); Virginia perch, mademoiselle, tint (312).

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial:  Generally too small in size to support a commercial fishery (834).  No special fishery exists because stocks have declined in recent years (791), and Florida landings data do not list the species separately (902).  Caught with pound nets, seines and bottom trawls, but only occasionally marketed for human consumption (791).  Hildebrand and Schroeder (312) reported that in the early 1920's, small quantities of larger fish were sold in the markets at Norfolk and Baltimore.

Recreational:  Caught by sport fishermen by hook and line, but used mostly for bait (791). Considered an excellent pan fish comparable to Spot (834).

Ecological Role:  In several systems the silver perch may become a dominant species (648) and therefore have an enormous effect on the ecology of a system.

Indicator:  Hansen and Wilson (272) recorded concentrations of DDT and its metabolites from .02 to 1.26 in 0 class fish from Pensacola estuary.

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall:  In the western Atlantic from Massachusetts and Connecticut to southern Florida, and in the eastern and northern Gulf of Mexico from Florida to northern Mexico (788 791).  Very abundant from New Jersey to central Florida .  In the northern Gulf of Mexico,  Hoese and Moore (327) reported that silver perch are more common to saltier bays, with young occurring in grass beds, which might indicate a greater abundance toward south Texas.

Within Study Area:  Common in nearshore and estuarine waters throughout Florida, with young found mostly in estuarine grass beds (993), also reported from fresh waters (791 1037).  Abundant year round in Charlotte Harbor (789), and common especially during warmer months in Tampa Bay and at Cedar Key (581 664).  Found throughout the Indian River Lagoon, but the largest abundance occurs in the north and central part of the lagoon (993 997 1195 1196 1242) with very few occurring in the southern end of the Indian River Lagoon (887).

Mobility and Migration:

sections.heading: Life Mode
sections.content: Eggs are pelagic (392 415), larvae pelagic to demersal, juveniles and adults are demersal (363).

sections.heading: Movement/Migration
sections.content: Silver Perch adults move to deeper bay waters and offshore in winter, returning to the estuarine feeding and nursery grounds in the spring and summer to spawn (171 255 791).  In the Maryland _ Virginia area, most commonly taken in the bays from May through October (312 886 1057).  Abundant in North Carolina sounds and estuaries from early spring to late fall (834).  Juveniles move into the shallow back bays (255).  In Tampa Bay, young appear in Boca Ciega Bay in May; by June, they begin to appear in Tampa Bay while remaining fairly abundant in Boca Ciega Bay.  Numbers taken in Tampa Bay increase considerably in July, and begin decreasing by August; most are gone from the bay by November (664).

sections.heading: BENTHIC HABITAT
sections.content:
Habitat Type:  Eggs may be estuarine to marine depending on where they are spawned (363).  Adults most common in bays and quiet lagoons, especially estuaries (171).  Reid (581) considered the species to be primarily an open water inhabitant at Cedar Key.

Substrate:  Adults over mud and sand bottoms (602 791).  Juveniles found along shore zone rivers in ditches, in lower portions of marsh creeks over mud and sand bottoms (725) often over heavy detritus (313); young usually occur in grass bed areas (327).

sections.heading: Temperature
sections.content: Larvae have been taken in temperatures from 16.4 - 31.8 (354).  In Charlotte Harbor, small specimens (11 - 25 mm SL) were taken at 16.1 C (789).   Juveniles have been taken in temperatures ranging from 4.8 C (725) to 32.5 C (664).  Adults have been collected at temperatures from 10.0 - 34.5 C (255 603 789).  Springer and Woodburn (664) reported cold killed individuals in Tampa Bay when water temperature was recorded as 13.0 C, however Gilmore et al. (236) reported none killed in an Indian River Lagoon hypothermal mortality where minimum temperatures ranged from 6 to 13 C.

sections.heading: Salinity
sections.content: Larvae have been taken at salinities from 2.0 (1007) to 37.4 ppt (363).  Juveniles and/or adults found in several locations at salinities from 0.0 (264 725 789 848 885 1043) to 35.0 ppt (255 581 664 751 789).  Adults are euryhaline, taken in salinities from 0.0 - 48.0 ppt (171 255 751 1043).

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content: Reproductive Mode:  The species is dioecious with broadcast spawning and external fertilization.

sections.heading: Mating/Spawning
sections.content:
As with most of the drums sound produced by special muscles inserted at the swim bladder wall are believed to play a role in the spawning activity (246 1058 1059).  Spawning probably occurs in primary bays and passes (255 313 614 664 725 1058), but may also occur offshore to some extent since eggs have been collected there (116 313).  Reported season is March through May in Tampa Bay (664), May to September in northern Florida (581), April through June in Louisiana (252 614 751), and the spring in Texas (255).  Gilmore (1271) has heard male spawning sounds during all months of the year.  Spawning peaks may occur in spring and late summer (116).  In the Atlantic, spawning occurs in New Jersey from June through August with a peak in June (762), in the spring and early summer (May - July) in Delaware and Chesapeake Bays (312 368), and in April through mid-July in North Carolina (313).  It has been suggested that spawning occurs in the early evening before 8 o'clock (393).  Ripe individuals or eggs collected at 14.3 - 26.0 ppt and 19.40 C - 28.0 C (363).

Fecundity: A 140 mm female was reported to contain 52,000 eggs (312).

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Egg/Larvae:  Range of total egg diameter 0.66 - 0.88mm (mean 0.69 - 0.83mm) (368).  Eggs reported to hatch in about 18 hours at 27.0 C (393), and in 40 - 50 hours at 19.0 to 21.0 C (762).  Yolksac larvae hatch at 1.5 - 1.9 mm (762).  Two days after hatching yolk sac completely absorbed, and larvae measure 2.5 - 2.8 mm (392 762).  Notochord flexion begins at 3.5 - 5.0 mm and is completed by 7.0 - 8.0 mm (392).

Juveniles/Adults:  The juvenile stage is attained around 10 mm TL (392).  Juveniles exhibit growth rates of about 15 mm/month from May to November (116).  Hildebrand and Cable (313) reported the following average lengths at Beaufort:  June, 8.7 mm; July, 31.9 mm; September, 81 mm; February 117.5 mm.  The following lengths were reported from Beaufort and the Chesapeake areas: first winter, 60 - 140 mm; second winter, 120 - 200 mm; and third season at spawning, 150 - 210 mm (392).  Some individuals may mature at the end of their first year (313) but most mature during their second year (762).  Reported size at maturity 130 - 140 mm (255 313) to 150 - 210 mm (470 762).  Frequently reach a size of 240 mm (327 762), and largest individual reported as 300 mm (788).  May live up to 6 years (762).  Another study, conducted in Mexico, reports the maximum age as 13 months (Chavance et al. 1984)

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content: Silver Perch larvae and small juveniles consume mostly copepods (163).  Larger juveniles and adults are primarily carnivores, feeding mainly on small crustaceans and benthic invertebrates, and occasionally on small fishes (163 179 241 312 581 664 791).
